title: thank-you as a reflex

segments.voice: Yesterday: bismillah. In the name of God, said before a beginning. Did one ordinary thing get a breath before it started? Day three.

Ask a Muslim friend how they are. There's a good chance the first word back isn't fine. It's alhamdulillah. Got the job? Alhamdulillah. Didn't get the job? Very often, also alhamdulillah. Someone sneezes: alhamdulillah. A player scores and drops to the grass. A grandmother, asked about her knees, which are terrible: alhamdulillah. It comes out so fast it sounds like a reflex. It is one. But it's a reflex people choose to build, on purpose, and it points somewhere that surprises people. Today: the thank-you that isn't quite a thank-you.
screen: `HOW ARE YOU?` → `GOT THE JOB. DIDN'T GET THE JOB.` → `THE SAME WORD, EITHER WAY.`

segments.voice: Al-hamdu li-llah. Al: the. Hamd: praise. Li-llah: belongs to God. The praise belongs to God. Not thanks, God, exactly. Arabic has a separate word for thanks, shukr, and scholars draw the line between the two with care. Thanks answers something done for you. Praise answers who someone is. You can only give thanks for the good day. You can give praise on any day. That's why the word keeps showing up on the bad ones. The root of hamd, h-m-d, belongs to a family you've already heard of. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ carries it in his name: Muhammad means the one who is praised, again and again. Ahmad, Mahmoud, Hamid: the same three letters. The phrase sits near the very top of the Qur'an, right after the bismillah. We'll open that line together in a few days. And it's woven into the day. A hadith in Bukhari says: when you sneeze, say alhamdulillah, and whoever hears you answers, may God have mercy on you. After the prayer, many Muslims count it thirty-three times, on their fingers or on prayer beads. Sunni Muslims usually say it between two other short phrases; Shia Muslims say it in a sequence named for Fatima, the Prophet's daughter. Different orders, the same word. And a hadith in Muslim's collection explains why it fits any kind of day. The Prophet said the believer's situation is a wonder: when good comes, they're grateful, and that's good for them; when hardship comes, they're patient, and that's good for them too. Alhamdulillah is the two-second version. It doesn't pretend the bad day was good. It says the praise still belongs where it belonged this morning.
screen: `THE PRAISE BELONGS TO GOD.` · `PRAISE, NOT ONLY THANKS.` · `H-M-D — THE ROOT OF MUHAMMAD.` · `GOOD DAY OR HARD DAY, BOTH COUNT.` · then, large: `ALHAMDULILLAH.`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. On the first, think of one thing that went right today. On the second, one thing that didn't. On the third, hold both at once, the good one and the hard one, and notice they belong to the same day. If you want, let the word ride out on that last breath: alhamdulillah.
Alhamdulillah. The praise belongs to God. Praise, not only thanks, so it fits every kind of day. Third word.
Your line: praise, whatever the day did. Tonight, before you sleep, name one thing from today worth praising, even if the day mostly wasn't. Day three.

howItsDone: Muslims say alhamdulillah when asked how they are, after meals, after sneezing, and at good news and hard news alike; after the prayer many repeat it thirty-three times, counting on their fingers or prayer beads.

myth: alhamdulillah is only for good news
it's said on hard days too. praise answers who God is, not only what went well.
the name Muhammad shares a root with alhamdulillah
h-m-d: Muhammad means the one praised again and again.
hamd and shukr are two words for the same thing
shukr is thanks for something done; hamd is praise for who someone is.

fork.setup: you sneeze, and say alhamdulillah. a Muslim friend hears you. what does the hadith say they answer?
options: may God have mercy on you.
fork.reveal: may God have mercy on you: yarhamuk Allah. a hadith in Bukhari turns a sneeze into a small exchange of praise and blessing.

original.note: Arabic: "the praise belongs to God." al (the) + hamd (praise) + li-llah (to God).

trapdoor: what it means: the praise belongs to God — praise, which fits any day, not only thanks for a good one.
what a scholar hears: hamd and shukr are different words: shukr answers a favor, hamd answers who someone is. the root h-m-d also names the Prophet: Muhammad, the much-praised.
